summary: An eiruv may be made with any food except water and salt. The mishnah also teaches about maaser sheni money, a promise not to eat food, and making an eiruv for a nazir, a Yisrael and a Kohen.

chunks.en: We may make an eiruv and a shituf with any food,
chunks.explain: An eiruv lets us carry or walk farther on Shabbos.
chunks.st: One may establish a joining of houses in courtyards [eiruv ḥatzerot] in order to permit carrying on Shabbat in a courtyard shared by two or more houses, and one may establish a joining of Shabbat borders [eiruv teḥumin] in order to extend the distance one is permitted to walk on Shabbat; and similarly, one may merge courtyards in order to permit carrying in an alleyway shared by two or more courtyards. This may be done with all kinds of food

words.note: A shituf joins the courtyards of an alleyway with shared food.

chunks.en: except water and salt.
chunks.st: except for water and salt,
chunks.stMore: as they are not considered foods and therefore may not be used for these purposes.

chunks.en: And anything may be bought with maaser money,
chunks.st: The mishna continues with two similar principles: All types of food may be bought with second-tithe money,
chunks.stMore: which must be taken to Jerusalem and used to purchase food (Deuteronomy 14:26),

words.note: Maaser sheni money must be spent on food in Yerushalayim.

chunks.en: except water and salt.
chunks.st: except for water and salt.

chunks.en: Someone who promised not to eat food
chunks.st: Similarly, one who vows that nourishment is prohibited to him

chunks.en: may still have water and salt.
chunks.st: is permitted to eat water and salt,
chunks.stMore: as they are not considered sources of nourishment.

chunks.en: We may make an eiruv for a nazir with wine, and for a Yisrael with terumah.
chunks.explain: Even though they may not eat it, others may.
chunks.st: It was further stated with regard to the laws of joining courtyards that one may establish an eiruv teḥumin for a nazirite with wine, even though he is prohibited to drink it, because it is permitted to others. And similarly, one may establish an eiruv teḥumin for an Israelite with teruma,
chunks.stMore: even though he may not eat it, because it is permitted to a priest. The food used for an eiruv teḥumin must be fit for human consumption, but it is not essential that it be fit for the consumption of the one for whom it is being used.

words.note: A nazir promised not to drink wine.

chunks.en: Sumchos says,
chunks.st: Summakhos, however, says:

chunks.en: only with regular food. And for a Kohen we may make it in a beis hapras.
chunks.explain: A field where a grave was plowed up, which a Kohen may not enter.
chunks.st: One may only establish an eiruv teḥumin for an Israelite with unconsecrated food. It was additionally stated that one may establish an eiruv teḥumin for a priest in a beit haperas,
chunks.stMore: a field containing a grave that was plowed over. There is doubt as to the location of bone fragments in the entire area. A priest is prohibited to come into contact with a corpse, and therefore may not enter a beit haperas.

words.note: A field where a grave was plowed over, so bits of bone may be anywhere.

chunks.en: because he can go there with something blocking him and eat it.
chunks.st: in a graveyard, an area which the priest may not enter by Torah law, since he can interpose
chunks.stMore: between himself and the graves and go and eat the food that comprises the eiruv without contracting ritual impurity.

summary: An eiruv may be made with food that is now allowed to eat, but not with food that still needs terumah and maaser taken, or that still needs to be redeemed. The eiruv must be sent with a person who can be trusted to put it down.

chunks.st: One may establish an eiruv with demai,

chunks.en: and with maaser sheni and hekdesh that were redeemed.

chunks.st: it is a valid eiruv. The critical point in the establishment of an eiruv is that it must be deposited in the proper location by a competent person; but it is immaterial how the eiruv arrives there.

chunks.st: If one placed his eiruv in a tree

chunks.en: If he put it in a pit,
chunks.st: If he placed the eiruv in a pit,

chunks.stMore: so that he is now unable to open the cupboard and access the eiruv,

chunks.en: it is an eiruv.
chunks.st: it is nonetheless a valid eiruv.

chunks.en: Rabbi Eliezer says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Eliezer says:

chunks.en: if he does not know that the key is in its place,
chunks.st: If he does not know that the key is in its place,

chunks.en: it is not an eiruv.
chunks.st: it is not a valid eiruv.

summary: If something happened to the eiruv before Shabbos started, it does not work; if it happened after dark, it works. The Rabbis argue what to do when we are not sure when it happened.

chunks.en: If the eiruv rolled out past the Shabbos limit,
chunks.explain: The techum is how far we may walk on Shabbos, 2000 amos.
chunks.st: If one’s eiruv rolled beyond the Shabbat limit,

words.note: The techum is the limit of how far we may walk on Shabbos.

chunks.en: or a pile of stones fell on it,
chunks.st: and he no longer has access to his eiruv since he may not go beyond his limit, or if a pile of stones fell on it,

chunks.en: or it was burned,
chunks.st: or if it was burnt,

chunks.en: or it was terumah and became tamei,
chunks.st: or if the eiruv was teruma and it became ritually impure;

chunks.en: while it was still day,
chunks.st: if any of these occurrences took place while it was still day,
chunks.stMore: prior to the onset of Shabbat,

chunks.en: it is not an eiruv.
chunks.st: it is not a valid eiruv,
chunks.stMore: since one did not have an eiruv at twilight, which is the time one’s Shabbat residence is established.

chunks.en: If it happened after dark, it is an eiruv.
chunks.st: However, if any of these occurred after dark, when it was already Shabbat, it is a valid eiruv,
chunks.stMore: as it was intact and accessible at the time one’s Shabbat residence is determined.

chunks.en: If we are not sure,
chunks.st: If the matter is in doubt,
chunks.stMore: i.e., if he does not know when one of the aforementioned incidents occurred,

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah say,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say:

chunks.en: he is like a donkey driver and a camel driver.
chunks.explain: He is pulled both ways, so he may only walk where both places allow.
chunks.st: This person is in the position of both a donkey driver, who must prod the animal from behind, and a camel driver,
chunks.stMore: who must lead the animal from the front, i.e., he is a person who is pulled in two opposite directions. Due to the uncertainty concerning his Shabbat border, he must act stringently, as though his resting place were both in his town and at the location where he placed the eiruv. He must restrict his Shabbat movement to those areas that are within two thousand cubits of both locations.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon say,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon disagree and say:

words.note: A Rabbi who lived before the Mishnah was written.

chunks.en: that an eiruv we are not sure about is kosher.
chunks.st: that an eiruv whose validity is in doubt is valid.

summary: A person may put down two eiruvin, one on each side of town, and decide later which one counts, depending on which way enemies come from or where a Sage comes to.

chunks.st: A person may make a condition with regard to his eiruv

chunks.st: and say: If gentiles come from the east,

chunks.st: my eiruv is in the west,

chunks.en: If from the west,

chunks.st: If they come from here and from there,

chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: he may go wherever he wants.
chunks.st: he may go wherever he wishes.

chunks.st: Rabbi Eliezer says:

chunks.st: He or his agent brings

This being the case, you should also agree with me that one can make two separate eiruvin for the two days in two different directions.

summary: Long ago, people did not always know if Rosh Hashanah would be one day or two. Rabbi Yehudah says a person could make a different eiruv for each day, but the Sages did not agree.
stIntro: During the time period when the Jewish calendar was established by the court according to the testimony of witnesses who had seen the new moon, Rosh HaShana would be observed for only one day if witnesses arrived on that day, and for two days if witnesses failed to arrive and the month of Elul was declared to be an extended, thirty-day month.
